title: Pragmatic politics: Why Turkey avoids blaming Russia for Black Sea attacks
gist: Barin Kayaoglu argues that deadly Black Sea strikes on Turkish-linked ships, which left at least two dead and 10 missing in one week, are straining Turkey-Russia ties, but economic interests and Ankara's role as mediator between Moscow and the West make a rupture unlikely.

insights.claim: Ankara is unlikely to break with Moscow over Black Sea attacks on Turkish-linked vessels because of economic interests, active mediation efforts and its incentive to keep balancing between Russia and the West.
insights.so_what: Investors should not expect Turkey to join Western pressure on Russia; Turkish-Russian trade and energy links likely persist.
insights.quote: economic interests, active mediation efforts and Ankara’s incentive to preserve its balancing act between Moscow and the West make a rupture unlikely
insights.speaker: Barin Kayaoglu

insights.claim: Beyond economics, Turkey's restraint toward Russia is shaped by its aim to stay an indispensable mediator between the Kremlin and the West.
insights.so_what: Turkey's mediator role is a strategic asset it will protect, which limits its policy moves against Moscow.

insights.claim: In one week, a series of strikes on commercial vessels owned or operated by Turkish companies in the Black Sea killed at least two people, with 10 more crew members missing and feared dead.
insights.so_what: Rising lethality against commercial shipping pushes up war-risk insurance and freight costs for Black Sea routes.

insights.so_what: Ukrainian grain export flows via the Danube ports are exposed to attack, a risk for grain prices and shipping.
